idiom_name: framework-published API + DTO/mapper translation layer + written versioning policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: pick the protocol technology (HTTP/JSON with an OpenAPI document, gRPC with .proto, GraphQL SDL, or - for in-process consumers - a published API/ABI), declare the contract as a versioned artifact, and implement it as a thin surface whose handlers map wire DTOs to domain calls and back through one mapper layer. The internal model never appears in a signature, a schema or an exported symbol; anything the domain needs to change stays behind the seam. Evolution follows a written policy: add optional fields and capabilities inside the current version, keep every published shape valid, and start a new version only for a genuine break - keeping the old one served until consumers migrate, with deprecation marked in the schema. In most stacks the routing, serialisation and document generation are supplied by a framework; what is never supplied is the decision of what to expose and the discipline to keep idiosyncratic consumer needs out of the shared protocol.
pitfalls: Publishing the internal model as the protocol freezes it: every later domain refactoring becomes a wire-incompatible change.
Treating the protocol as documentation only - without a versioning policy and a deprecation window, the first incompatible change breaks all consumers at once.
Letting each consumer's special case into the shared protocol until it is a lowest-common-denominator surface; serve the idiosyncratic case with a one-off translator instead.

Treating the API version as a copy of every software release - or minting a new URI/version for each minor change - multiplies legacy surfaces and can orphan clients; evolve additively and introduce a new identifier only for a genuine incompatibility, while keeping the predecessor supported during migration.
